hook: Turn the pedals of a bike and the back wheel spins faster than your feet, because the gears multiply the rate. Many functions work the same way: one function feeds its output into another. The chain rule says the rates multiply, and it is the rule you will use most often for the rest of the course.

prereq.q: What is the derivative of $\sin x$?
prereq.why: The derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$.
The power rule: bring the 5 down and lower the power by one.

figure.caption: The inside function $2x$ squeezes $\sin x$ sideways by a factor of 2, so every slope doubles: at the origin the slope of $\sin(2x)$ is $2$, not $1$.

chain.cause: A function is built in layers, $h(x) = f(g(x))$
chain.effect: $x$ feeds the inside function $g$, and $g(x)$ feeds the outside function $f$

chain.cause: When $x$ changes a little, $g$ changes $g'(x)$ times as much
chain.effect: and $f$ changes $f'(g(x))$ times as much as its input $g$ does

chain.cause: The two rates multiply, like gears

ideas: Spot the layers first: name the outside function and the inside function before you differentiate.
Differentiate the outside function and leave the inside alone: $f'(g(x))$, not $f'(x)$ and not $f'(g'(x))$.
Then multiply by the derivative of the inside, $g'(x)$. Forgetting this factor is the most common lost point.
From a table, read $f'$ at the inside value $g(a)$, then multiply by $g'(a)$.

misconception.right: That is only the outside derivative. The inside function $x^2$ changes too, at rate $2x$, so $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x$.

summary: For a composite function $f(g(x))$, differentiate the outside function at the unchanged inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside: $\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$. Name the layers before you start, and never drop the inside derivative.
